kp.k: Oregon approved supervised practice as a licensure pathway
kp.d: The document reports that the Oregon Supreme Court approved the Supervised Practice Portfolio Examination (SPPE) in November 2023. Candidates may complete 675 hours under an experienced attorney’s supervision and submit a portfolio instead of taking the traditional bar exam. Gallini says eligibility extends to graduates of any ABA-accredited law school. The interview addresses licensure and professional formation, not AI.
qs: In November 2023 the Oregon Supreme Court approved a new pathway to becoming a licensed attorney: the **Supervised Practice Portfolio Examination** (SPPE).

Instead of taking the traditional bar exam, law students who hope to practice in Oregon may complete 675 hours of practice under the supervision of an experienced attorney and then submit a portfolio of work to the Board of Bar Examiners.
The grads who raise their hands, as you know, may not just be from Oregon as it’s open to graduates from any ABA-accredited law school.

kp.k: Pandemic diploma privilege prompted broader licensing reconsideration
kp.d: Gallini traces the task force’s origins to Oregon’s emergency diploma privilege in summer 2020, approved 4-to-3 for graduates of all three Oregon law schools. He reports subsequent increases in employment rates at those schools and employer satisfaction because hires could start without awaiting bar passage. These are reported observations without numerical estimates or a causal study supplied in the interview.
qs: Oregon was one of five jurisdictions that responded by granting emergency diploma privilege.
In that summer of 2020, the State Supreme Court voted 4-to-3 to grant emergency onetime diploma privilege to graduates of all three Oregon law schools.
We saw an increase in satisfaction from employers because they didn’t have to wait for their hires to begin work; normally, after all, their doing so would be contingent on passing the bar.

kp.k: Reform challenges the traditional exam’s privileged status
kp.d: Gallini rejects describing SPPE as an alternative because he believes that framing implies inferiority and exempts the existing exam from scrutiny. He reports public protection as the chief objection to reform, while interpreting some resistance as attachment to an ordeal incumbent lawyers themselves experienced. His response questions what the bar measures and whether legal education adequately prepares graduates to practise.
qs: It makes it look like it’s something less than the current bar exam.
Somewhat ironically, it lets the current bar exam totally off the hook.
On the task force, the chief objection we heard was that people distrusted whether something new would protect the public.
To some degree, the bar exam lets law schools off the hook in that regard.

kp.k: Bar preparation imposes unequal financial and caregiving burdens
kp.d: Drawing on conversations with unsuccessful examinees, Gallini argues that work and family obligations can prevent otherwise promising future attorneys from preparing adequately. He characterises the exam as favouring candidates with time and financial support. His own estimate of approximately $29,400 for one sitting includes preparation, lost wages, examination and associated fees, and living costs while awaiting results; it is not presented as a measured population average.
qs: I also talk about how the exam is one of privilege—it favors those who don’t have to work, those who don’t have families to care for, those who have the time to put in because of their life circumstances, and perhaps some candidates even have a job that is paying for their bar prep program and a living stipend.

It includes your bar provider, the lost wages because of the time you take away from working, the exam fee, character and fitness, the investigation, the laptop fee, then the living expense cost of waiting for the score.
I calculate sitting for one bar exam at around $29,400.

kp.k: Portfolio assessment connects entry competence to actual legal work
kp.d: Gallini describes SPPE as an examination of work products linked to skills the public should expect from newly licensed lawyers. The Board of Bar Examiners grades every portfolio item, rather than supervision alone establishing competence. He distinguishes readiness for first-year practice from lifelong expertise and argues that passing a one-time examination should not be treated as proof of permanent competence.
qs: Rather, it’s about tying the work that lawyers do with the skills that the public should expect newly licensed lawyers to have.
Each item of the portfolio is reviewed and graded by the Board of Bar Examiners, which is the same body that grades the current bar exam—a point that is often lost in some of the media conversation.
This is just what we think you should be able to do coming out of law school and being ready to contribute to the profession in your first year.

kp.k: Proposed monitoring lacks a comparable traditional-exam baseline
kp.d: Gallini says planned state-level monitoring concerns participation, practice destinations, major-firm hiring, demographic differences in pathway selection, and whether outcomes reproduce disparities associated with the current exam. He expects some IAALS support but warns that equivalent tracking is not conducted for the traditional exam, limiting a fair comparison. These are monitoring intentions and questions, not SPPE outcome findings.
qs: The court, and I think the public generally, is interested in where they will practice.
Then I think there are some questions around will there be any race-, gender-, or ethnicity-based distinctions in who selects this path?
If we’re really serious about launching the SPPE and giving it a fair shake, we should probably be doing the exact same thing with the current bar exam.
But I don’t see us, unfortunately, doing that tracking for the current bar exam.

kp.k: Success includes interstate recognition and rural attorney recruitment
kp.d: Gallini proposes three broad success criteria: continued licensure-reform discussions beyond Oregon, portability or recognition of SPPE in other states, and improved rural recruitment. He proposes a postgraduate fellowship allowing graduates to work in high-need areas while becoming licensed. He presents licensure as a possible tool for addressing rural access, immigration representation and public defense needs, not as an already demonstrated solution.
qs: The first is a shift in the conversation around attorney licensure.
The second would be some level of portability, reciprocity, or recognition of passing the SPPE in other states.
The third major measure of success would be making a difference in recruiting in rural areas.

I would like to leverage the SPPE to serve high-need areas by creating a postgraduate fellowship where a new law graduate could go to a high-need area, become licensed, and take that experience into their next job.

kp.k: Licensure reform requires curricular alignment and graduate course access
kp.d: Gallini reports that Willamette has aligned its curriculum with court-required SPPE prerequisites and launched JD for Life so graduates, including those from other schools nationwide, can take missing prerequisite courses. He recommends designing course groupings around assessed practice skills while retaining traditional bar-related teaching because SPPE coexists with the current examination.
qs: What we have to do is make sure that we stand up a curriculum that matches what the court has said students are required to take in order to be eligible to pursue SPPE.
We launched something that we call “JD for Life” that will address this need, and it’s open to graduates across the country.
The SPPE does not disrupt the current bar exam.
But we need to think with intention about stable buckets of courses that are reverse-engineered to teach the skills that will be tested in the SPPE.

kp.k: Experiential teaching changes faculty deployment and classroom economics
kp.d: Gallini advocates greater investment in clinics, externships and simulations and reports efforts to strengthen experiential offerings and incentivise faculty participation. His illustrative criminal-procedure simulation would have students negotiate guilty pleas and appear before him as judge. He contrasts the cost-effectiveness of a 100-plus-student lecture course with his preferred simulation size of about 20, identifying faculty-resource implications rather than reporting measured instructional outcomes.
qs: In law schools, that means investing more into experiential learning, including clinics, externships, and simulation learning.
We’ve been spending a lot of time strengthening current experiential offerings on a more regularized basis as well as encouraging and incentivizing faculty to build out more experiential offerings.
I mentioned the number of students intentionally because, wearing my dean hat, it’s much more cost-effective to put 100+ in my Crim Pro II podium-style class.
I think 20 is probably the right number for that class—it’s more students than we would enroll in a clinic, but fewer than in a traditional podium classroom.

kp.k: Judicial openness enabled reform; service pressures possibly encouraged it
kp.d: Gallini credits the Oregon Supreme Court’s willingness to reconsider licensing as essential. Explicitly identifying his explanation as speculation, he suggests Oregon’s immigration-representation commitment and public defense crisis encouraged openness to reform. He hopes Oregon’s example will make other jurisdictions more willing to reconsider established licensing practices.
qs: I think the credit overwhelmingly has to go to the Oregon Supreme Court.
I think, and now I’m entering more speculation mode, the subtext of what’s been happening here locally in the state matters.
But we’re also in the middle of a public defense crisis.
So between those two major issues, I think there was a willingness to think a little bit differently about how to serve Oregonians.
As a profession, we’re so wedded to doing it the way we’ve always done it.
